videoIdeas.title: You can't speak because you never practise being uncomfortable
videoIdeas.hook: The amount of people who can't string a sentence together in front of others is genuinely alarming.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your public speaking take (DbilFRjsJ3v) got 619 views with 0 comments — the idea landed but the execution was flat. Meanwhile saffanabanana is pulling 30k+ on communication content with punchy, prescriptive hooks like 'Stop writing like that.' There's a clear gap: you own the 'young Muslims can't communicate' angle but you're not being prescriptive enough. Turn the complaint into a method.
videoIdeas.script:
The amount of people who can't string a sentence together in front of others is genuinely alarming.

And it's not because you're 'shy'. It's because the last time you spoke to a stranger without a screen in front of you was in 2019.

Speaking isn't a talent. It's a muscle. You've just never trained it.

So here's the fix, and it costs you nothing. Once a day, have one conversation you'd normally avoid. Order at the counter instead of the app. Ask the shopkeeper a real question. Speak up in the group when you'd usually stay quiet.

That's it. You're not born eloquent. You get eloquent by being willing to be a bit awkward first.

The ones who lead the room later are just the ones who were comfortable sounding stupid earlier.

visuals.setting: Standing, mid-frame, plain wall or outdoors in the city. Casual smart — no set, no ring light theatrics. Direct eye contact, calm but firm energy, like you're calling someone out but for their own good.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text punchline appears as you speak: 'You're not shy. You're just untrained.' — held for the first 3 seconds while you deliver the opening line.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-sentence with no intro, jump straight to 'because you never practise being uncomfortable'
Pattern interrupt: hold up your phone, then put it face-down on a table as you say the first line
Silent count on screen '1 conversation a day' ticking up as a visual anchor

videoIdeas.title: Leadership is competence + trust, in that order
videoIdeas.hook: Everyone wants to be listened to. Almost nobody wants to earn the right to be.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your Prophetic leadership post (DTauCL6jJ8Z, 'Al-Qawi wal-Ameen') got 508 views and only 1 comment — solid but under-leveraged. doctordaanish's 'save this' listicles and lifeofdinoo's short question hooks are dominating. Repackage your strongest leadership idea into a tighter, more quotable frame so it travels.
videoIdeas.script:
Everyone wants to be listened to. Almost nobody wants to earn the right to be.

The Qur'an gives you the formula in two words: Al-Qawi wal-Ameen. Strong and trustworthy. Competent and honest.

Notice the order. Competence first. Because a trustworthy man who can't do the job is useless, and a competent man you can't trust is dangerous.

You want people to follow you? Stop asking for influence. Go and get good at something real. Then be the kind of person who doesn't need watching.

That's leadership. Everything else is just a loud voice with nothing behind it.

visuals.setting: Seated, slightly closer framing, calmer and more deliberate delivery — this is the 'sit down and listen' pillar. Neutral background, maybe a bookshelf. Lower energy than the callout videos, more weight.
visuals.visualHook: Two words appear on screen big and bold — 'STRONG' then 'TRUSTWORTHY' — snapping in one after the other as you say them, over the opening line.
otherHookIdeas: On-screen text: 'You don't have a talent problem. You have an order problem.'
Cold open on the phrase 'Al-Qawi wal-Ameen' with Arabic text on screen, then translate
Hold up two fingers, count them down as you list competence then trust

videoIdeas.title: Stop performing outrage and do one useful thing
videoIdeas.hook: You've posted six times about the Ummah this week. What have you actually done?
videoIdeas.rationale: This is your proven lane — your top posts (DZTRC2KMKuU at 1045 views, DZ-25_MMv-v) are exactly this energy: calling out people who spew online while the Ummah suffers. But redirect it from pure refutation toward a mindset/action frame so it builds people up instead of just dunking. This keeps your best-performing subject while nudging it toward your pillars.
videoIdeas.script:
You've posted six times about the Ummah this week. Let me ask you something. What have you actually done?

Because outrage is cheap. It feels like action. It gives you the same rush. But at the end of the day you've moved nothing except your thumb.

Does it not shame you to spew your venom while your brothers and sisters are being attacked left, right and centre?

Here's the swap. For every post you write about a problem, do one real thing. Donate. Show up. Learn something you can actually teach. Speak to someone who needs it.

The Ummah doesn't need more commentators. It's drowning in them. It needs people who close the laptop and go be useful.

visuals.setting: Standing, outdoors or in a real everyday location — not a studio. Higher energy, direct, this is the confrontational older-brother tone your audience already responds to. Look slightly annoyed but controlled.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text counter: '6 posts this week' with a red strikethrough appearing over it as you deliver the opening question.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-argument: start on 'What have you actually done?' with no lead-in
Pattern interrupt: close a laptop lid hard on camera as the first frame
On-screen punchline text: 'Outrage isn't action. It just feels like it.'

videoIdeas.title: Third spaces are the most important thing you're ignoring
videoIdeas.hook: Young British Muslims are quietly building the thing the community's been crying about for years.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your third-spaces post (Dbwq4JosFxD, 890 views) is one of your few genuinely constructive, forward-looking posts and it performed well with low comments — meaning it resonated but didn't spark discussion. Lean into it harder as a leadership/community-building message. It's timely, it's positive, and it separates you from pure hot-take accounts.
videoIdeas.script:
Young British Muslims are quietly building the thing the community's been crying about for years. And barely anyone's clapping.

Cafés. Study circles. Community hubs. Social events. Actual spaces where people can meet, build something, and belong.

And instead of backing it, half of you are online picking it apart. Too casual. Not serious enough. Not 'Islamic' enough for your taste.

Understand this. A generation that has somewhere to belong doesn't get radicalised by loneliness. It doesn't disappear into a screen. It builds.

So if you can't build one, at least don't tear down the people who are. Support it, show up to it, or stay quiet. Those are your three options.

visuals.setting: Film in an actual café or community space if possible — B-roll of people talking, tables, tea. You speaking to camera in that environment, warmer energy than the callout videos. This one is about belonging, so the setting should feel alive.
visuals.visualHook: Cold open on B-roll of a busy café / gathering with on-screen text: 'This is leadership. You just didn't recognise it.'
otherHookIdeas: On-screen text: '3 options' appearing early to promise structure
Walk-and-talk through the space as the first shot
Punchline text overlay: 'Loneliness radicalises. Belonging builds.'

videoIdeas.title: You keep chasing influence before character
videoIdeas.hook: You want the audience before you've built anything worth listening to.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your caption 'We often chase influence before character' (DTauCL6jJ8Z) is one of the sharpest lines you've written and deserves its own dedicated video. This is a mindset piece that speaks directly to your audience of aspiring young Muslims who want to 'grow a platform'. It's evergreen and it's you at your most quotable — a gap because most of your recent content is reactive commentary, not standalone principles.
videoIdeas.script:
You want the audience before you've built anything worth listening to. That's the problem with your whole generation, and honestly, with mine too.

We chase influence before character. Followers before substance. The stage before the work.

But here's what nobody tells you. Influence with no character behind it is a liability. The bigger your reach, the faster people find out you're empty.

Character is the thing that survives the audience finding out who you really are.

So build the private version of yourself first. The one nobody's watching. Get that right, and the influence, if it ever comes, won't destroy you.

Most people online are one honest conversation away from being exposed. Don't be one of them.

visuals.setting: Seated, close, quieter and more reflective delivery — this is a 'talking to you directly' piece. Minimal background. Let the words carry it, no gimmicks. Slow, deliberate pacing.
visuals.visualHook: Plain black screen for half a second with white text 'Character > influence' before cutting to your face on the opening line — a hard visual pattern interrupt.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-thought on 'That's the problem with your whole generation'
On-screen text builds a list live: 'Followers before substance / stage before work'
End-card punchline text: 'Character survives the audience.'

videoIdeas.title: How to actually disagree without sounding like an idiot
videoIdeas.hook: Half of you don't have opinions. You have reactions you haven't thought through.
videoIdeas.rationale: You clearly love the refutation/disagreement space (multiple posts about people 'showing how dumb they can be'), but you could productise that instinct into a communication skill — how to argue well. This blends your public speaking pillar with your proven appetite for the discourse. It's a format saffanabanana wins with: prescriptive communication advice delivered bluntly.
videoIdeas.script:
Half of you don't have opinions. You have reactions you haven't thought through, dressed up as opinions.

And it shows the second you have to defend one. You get loud, you get personal, you bring up something from three arguments ago. That's not debate. That's panic.

So here's how to disagree like someone worth taking seriously.

One. Say back their point better than they said it. If you can't, you don't understand it yet, so sit down.

Two. Attack the argument, never the person. The moment you insult them, you've admitted you've run out of points.

Three. Be willing to lose. If you'd never change your mind, you're not discussing, you're performing.

Master that and you'll win more rooms than the loudest person in them ever will.

visuals.setting: Standing, mid-frame, sharp confident energy — this is you in your element. Plain background so the numbered points land. Use hand gestures to mark each point clearly.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text: 'reaction ≠ opinion' snaps up as you say the first line, big and bold.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-point: start on 'you get loud, you get personal' then reset
Numbered on-screen text (1, 2, 3) appearing to promise a clear structure
Punchline overlay: 'Insult = you've run out of points'

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your all-time top post at 6134 views — nearly double your next best. The reason is the hook: 'Can't believe we're still discussing the necessity of protests in 2026' opens mid-frustration, gives a clear stance, and taps a live, high-emotion topic. This is proof your audience rewards a strong, timely opinion delivered with conviction, not hedging.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: The caption trails off ('to make themselves feel bett...') and the value ends with the dunk. It got 211 likes but only 15 comments — high agreement, low discussion. Add a genuine question or a call to actually do something at the end to convert outrage into conversation and shares, not just nods.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your clearest public-speaking pillar post — 'the amount of people that struggle to string a sentence together is shocking' is a strong, relatable observation and exactly your niche. The nostalgia angle (people used to go outside and interact) is a good frame.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 619 views and 0 comments — it diagnosed a problem but gave nobody anything to do. It reads as a complaint, not advice. Add one concrete, actionable fix (like 'one uncomfortable conversation a day') so people save and share it instead of just agreeing silently. Prescriptive beats observational in this lane.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: The line 'We often chase influence before character' is one of your most quotable, and 'Al-Qawi wal-Ameen — competent and trustworthy' gives the audience a memorable, tweetable framework. This is your leadership pillar at its best: rooted in the deen, applicable, and distinct from the reactive commentary crowd.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 508 views and 1 comment means the idea deserved more reach than it got. The '📖 11 Prophetic Qualities' framing buries the strongest hook at the bottom. Lead with 'You chase influence before character' as the first line — the principle is stronger than the source citation for stopping the scroll.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Your most constructive, forward-looking post — 'Young British Muslims are creating third spaces' celebrates something real instead of just refuting. It's a needed break from the callout content and positions you as someone who builds, not just critiques. 890 views on a positive message is a good sign this audience wants more than outrage.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Only 2 comments — the positive framing didn't provoke discussion the way your dunks do. End with a mild challenge ('support it, show up, or stay quiet — pick one') to give people a stance to react to. You can keep the constructive tone and still create friction that drives comments.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 'Don't let sectarianism blind you to the horrors that occurred in our Ummah' pulled 24 comments on 827 views — one of your best comment-to-view ratios. Tackling a genuinely divisive intra-community topic with a clear moral stance is what sparks real discussion, not just likes. This is your engagement formula.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: The 42 likes vs 24 comments split suggests it's divisive rather than agreeable — fine, but make sure the video itself lands the nuance so you're not just farming argument. Pin a comment that states your position clearly so the thread stays anchored to your point instead of descending into sectarian back-and-forth you didn't intend.
